title: Judgement
author: Dr. Ian Hallett
summary: Part two of a five-part series on Ian Hallett's Leadership Operating System, this piece takes judgement as the domain of reasoning and choosing well when information is incomplete and consequences are slow to appear. Hallett opens with Netflix's 2011 price rise and Qwikster reversal to ask whether it was bad judgement or good judgement badly carried out, and argues that results measure judgement and luck together. Drawing on overconfidence research by Moore and Healy and forecasting research by Mellers and colleagues, he claims that judgement can only be checked if it is written down in advance. His practical tool is a five-line decision note covering the underlying problem, assumptions, options, trade-offs and confidence. He then lists sixteen behaviours across diagnosis, strategic reasoning and decision discipline, names four common failure modes, and replays Netflix through the note using only public information.
points: Results reflect judgement and luck together, so leaders need a record of what they expected before the outcome arrives.
The five-line decision note forces a leader to state the underlying problem, assumptions, options considered, what is being given up, and a numeric confidence.
Sixteen behaviours sit under three disciplines: diagnosis, strategic and systemic reasoning, and decision discipline.
Four typical failures are the single option, the confident guess, the reopened decision and the comfortable wait.
The note is meant only for decisions that are costly to get wrong or hard to reverse; cheap, reversible decisions should be made in minutes.
quotes: Nobody can check your judgement until you write it down, including you.
Judgement can only be checked if you state what you expect, and how sure you are, before the result arrives.
My sense is that capable people are judged on results for so long that they start to treat results as the measure of their judgement. Results measure judgement and luck together.
A note with only one option in line three is a recommendation looking for approval. Line four is the one I see left blank most often, because the cost is the part nobody wants to say out loud.
A number makes your confidence something you can be wrong about, which is how you find out whether your nine-in-ten calls come true nine times in ten.
If you cannot name the fact that would change your mind, you already have enough information and are delaying.
The comfortable wait. One more report, one more month, because deciding feels riskier than waiting. Waiting has costs too, and nobody writes them down
